Meta released its open-weight Muse Glimmer model while Mark Zuckerberg argued for “superintelligence for all.” The release distributes capability. The essay treats that as distributed control.

That is the category error.

Open weights give more people agency. They do not give them the doctrine, evaluations, permissions, feedback paths, or accountability needed to govern what that agency does. You can put more pilots in the air without building more air traffic control.

A real balance of power requires regulatory capacity to spread with capability. Otherwise the gap widens between who can act and who can detect, stop, and repair the consequences.

Serious operators should judge an open model by the correction architecture around it—not by how many people can download it.

Photograph: Nic Coury/AP Mark Zuckerberg Zuckerberg pushes ‘superintelligent’ AI for all as Meta releases open-weight model Meta CEO presents utopian vision of AI in 6,000-word essay amid Silicon Valley debate over government regulation Nick Robins-Early Mon 10 Aug 2026 18.57 EDT Last modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 12.38 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Mark Zuckerberg published a lengthy essay on Monday detailing his views on artificial intelligence and announced several plans for how Meta would develop the technology in the future. The CEO’s essay went online the same day as Meta released a new, open-weight AI model that seeks to rival Anthropic and OpenAI’s products called Muse Glimmer. Over the course of more than 6,000 words in a post titled The Future is for Everyone, Zuckerberg addressed a range of topics related to AI that included datacenters, government regulation, cybersecurity, the creation of bioweapons, labor market disruption, surveillance powers and more. The essay presented a utopian vision of AI as a personalized “superintelligence” – using the word 60 times. “Some argue that superintelligence itself or a small set of experts who control it should decide what is best for humanity. We disagree,” Zuckerberg wrote. Central to Zuckerberg’s post was an argument for free-to-download, open-weight AI models – like the kind Meta develops – and a lack of government regulation of artificial intelligence. Zuckerberg’s stance sets him and Meta apart from industry leaders OpenAI and Anthropic, which have argued that open-source AI is dangerous. The two frontier labs have released proprietary AI products and argued that cutting-edge models should remain tightly controlled by the companies that build them. Crew of Zuckerberg yacht did not hear radio call to assist boat, Meta says Read more Zuckerberg’s post comes as Silicon Valley is engaged in a heated debate over how to regulate AI development, which has involved the creation of a secret White House framework for testing new models and an ongoing debate over whether to restrict the use of Chinese-made open-source AI. As Anthropic and OpenAI have surged ahead in the AI industry, competitors such as Meta have also grown wary of their dominance and sought to position their open models as alternatives. Zuckerberg framed Meta’s pursuit of open-weight AI as a more democratic version of the technology and one that will create a “balance of power” between users, whether that involves states, companies or individuals. His plans also called for letting users decide what “values” an AI model should have, as opposed to a company encoding it with rigid guardrails and beliefs. An AI agent for all? Try using your brain, Mark Zuckerberg Read more “If the power of superintelligence is held by a small number of individuals, businesses, governments, or AI itself, then that will naturally lead to outcomes that are less favorable for everyone else,” Zuckerberg wrote. Tech leaders have made a cottage industry out of releasing broad, vaguely philosophical treatises on artificial intelligence, which tend to double as marketing materials for their own companies and products. Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Palantir’s Alex Karp and the venture capitalist Marc Andreessen have all written long manifestos on the virtues and dangers of the technology. In addition to weighing in on open-source models, Zuckerberg also called for accelerating the buildout of AI infrastructure such as datacenters . The massive development of resource-hungry datacenters has become a divisive issue in the US, with rapidly growing public opposition and calls from politicians to issue moratoriums on their construction. Zuckerberg wrote in the essay that Meta would create a fund to invest more in local communities near datacenters, ands cited an example from Louisiana where some teachers received a $50,000 bonus check as a result of increased sales tax revenue from the company’s infrastructure investment. On government testing of AI models for cybersecurity risks, a tangible concern after rogue models have hacked outside organizations in recent months, Zuckerberg agreed that companies should share “intermediate training checkpoints and technical staff” but provided few details. He broadly warned that regulation would cause China to overtake the US in the AI race, where he claimed it already has an advantage in terms of building infrastructure. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to TechScape A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion Bernie Sanders calls on Silicon Valley to ‘pause AI development’ in interest of humanity Read more “Any policy that slows American model releases – even by a month – could add significant risk to American leadership while letting foreign models race ahead,” Zuckerberg. Many of Zuckerberg’s policy plans in his essay lacked detail or reiterated previous claims about the abundant wealth and prosperity that AI would create, such as touting that everyone would have “invention superpowers” to create new businesses. His version of the future also is inherently tied to Meta products, such as the company’s AI-enabled smart glasses. “Everyone will have an exceptionally capable personal agent that understands you, your goals, and everything you care about,” Zuckerberg said. “You’ll be able to interact with your agent through any device, including your glasses to keep you present in the moment with the people you care about.” On thornier issues such as loss of jobs from AI, autonomous weapons and government surveillance, Zuckerberg mostly brushed them aside. Law enforcement and the military already possess greater intelligence-gathering powers than the average person, Zuckerberg argued, and this would continue with access to AI. Companies may shrink in size due to AI, he conceded, but the technology would create new economic opportunities. “People will have to adapt, and this will be challenging,” Zuckerberg said about labor disruption from new technology. “But the more that everyone has a personal agent that is superintelligent at teaching us new skills and helping us adapt to change, the smoother this will be.” This article was amended on 12 August 2026. An earlier version of the headline and text said that Meta was releasing an open-source AI model; the company released an open-weight model. Join now 3,000 firms Independent Trusted Save up to 70% on staff Get 3 Quotes News » AI-linked layoffs hit 205,000 workers in 2026: report AI-linked layoffs hit 205,000 workers in 2026: report Danica Macayan Posted on August 12, 2026 2 min read Copied URL COLORADO, UNITED STATES — Artificial intelligence (AI)-attributed layoffs in the United States reached 205,000 workers through August 2026, with automation explicitly cited in more than half of all major documented workforce reductions across technology, finance, and professional services. The 2026 AI-linked total has already matched the equivalent full-year 2025 figure in less than eight months, reflecting an accelerating pace of automation-driven restructuring across United States employers. AI surpasses economic factors as top stated layoff reason ResumePulse ‘s August 2026 tracker found that AI or automation was cited as a primary or contributing driver in job losses affecting 205,000 workers across the United States, with cuts concentrated in customer service, data operations, entry-level software roles, and finance back offices. The firm reported that the share of organizations citing AI in layoff announcements had more than doubled since January 2026, with May and June recording the highest monthly AI-cited job-cut totals in the tracker’s history. The report attributed the acceleration to a convergence of factors: AI tools reaching operational maturity in back-office workflows, post-pandemic overstaffing corrections now using AI as both a catalyst and a cover, and tightening earnings pressure in sectors such as finance and technology. AI-focused outsourcing providers have seen demand rise in parallel, as companies seek outside partners to manage AI tool deployment rather than build internal teams. At 205,000 workers, AI-attributed job losses in 2026 have already matched or exceeded the full prior-year total in fewer than eight months. Outplacement data flags AI as top layoff driver Challenger, Gray & Christmas reported that AI was the leading stated reason for corporate job cuts in March and April 2026, marking the first time a technology factor topped its monthly layoff-rationale rankings. The outplacement firm tracked AI-cited business process outsourcing (BPO)-adjacent function cuts approaching 49,000 positions through mid-year, with the monthly pace accelerating as technology, retail, and financial services companies reported strong earnings alongside headcount reductions. Workers displaced from customer service, compliance, and data-processing roles face the narrowest re-entry opportunities, as those are precisely the functions where AI tools have shown the most immediate and measurable productivity gains. sources.content_text: Advisory Strategy Chief AI Speaking Governance AI-Marketing AI Workshops Copilot Tips ChatGPT Leadership Industries Engineering AI Implementation About Contact Blog Layout Microsoft Copilot Updates Aug 2026 August 13, 2026 Microsoft Copilot Updates August 2026: The Must-Have Changes for Business More than three years after Microsoft first introduced Bing Chat in February 2023, and as we approach the third anniversary of the Copilot brand, it is remarkable how quickly the platform has evolved. Microsoft Copilot started largely as an AI assistant you could ask to summarise a document, draft an email or answer a question. The August 2026 updates show Microsoft pushing Copilot towards something much bigger: an AI layer that can work across applications, organisational data, agents and business workflows. There are plenty of new features, but from an AI adoption perspective, not all of them matter equally. These are the five August updates I believe business and technology leaders should be paying attention to. 1. Excel Is Becoming One of Copilot's Most Powerful Business Tools For many organisations, Excel may end up being one of the most valuable places to use Microsoft Copilot. The latest capabilities move Copilot well beyond simply asking it to analyse a spreadsheet. Users can increasingly apply AI directly within their data, receive formula assistance, bring information from other documents into an analysis and use different approaches for exploring, planning and editing work. Use AI directly within spreadsheet workflows. Identify trends, anomalies and patterns faster. Bring information from other files and documents into an analysis. Support repeatable analytical and reporting tasks. My advice: don't train employees on Excel Copilot as a generic feature. Train them using their actual reports, data and recurring business tasks. 2. Copilot Is Starting to Take Action, Not Just Give Answers One of the most important changes is the shift from Copilot telling you what needs to happen towards helping you actually do it. Outlook is a good example. Copilot is becoming increasingly capable of supporting actions around meetings, scheduling, email follow-ups and administrative workflows. Strategically, this matters because the next phase of workplace AI isn't simply content generation. It's task execution. Think about how much time organisations collectively spend coordinating meetings, responding to email, following up actions and moving information between systems. These aren't glamorous use cases, but the productivity opportunity is substantial. 3. Copilot Is Moving Deeper Into Word and PowerPoint The future of Copilot isn't employees spending all day inside a separate chat window. It is Copilot increasingly working inside the applications where the work already happens. Word is becoming more useful for reviewing, rewriting and improving existing documents, while PowerPoint is getting better at creating presentations using organisational content, templates and branding. That's far more useful than generating a generic presentation or document and then spending another hour fixing it. One of the most important Copilot skills is therefore becoming: which Copilot experience should I use for this task? 4. Copilot Is Becoming More Flexible About the AI Behind It Another significant development is Microsoft's move towards greater flexibility in the AI models and specialist capabilities available through Copilot. Different models may be better suited to different types of work, whether that's complex reasoning, research, analysis, writing or working with long documents. I don't believe most employees need to become experts in foundation models. But they do need to understand that Copilot is increasingly becoming an orchestration layer rather than one fixed AI experience. The practical skill isn't knowing every model. It's knowing how to choose the right Copilot experience, agent or tool for the job. 5. Agents Are Moving Copilot From Tasks to Workflows This is the development I think executives should watch most closely. Copilot is increasingly moving from completing isolated tasks towards coordinating multiple steps using agents and connected Microsoft 365 capabilities. Instead of simply asking Copilot to summarise a meeting, think about a workflow where AI reviews the meeting, identifies actions, prepares follow-up communication, creates tasks and updates the relevant project information. That's the shift from individual productivity to workflow productivity — and I believe that's where much of the real economic value of Copilot will eventually sit. Key Takeaways From the August 2026 Copilot Updates Excel is becoming a much more important Copilot productivity environment. Copilot is increasingly taking actions rather than simply generating answers. In-app Copilot experiences are becoming more important than standalone chat alone. Users will increasingly need to understand which Copilot experience, model or agent fits each task. The biggest opportunity is moving from individual productivity towards collaborative and workflow productivity. The Biggest Copilot Update Isn't a Feature For me, the most important takeaway from the August updates isn't Excel, Outlook, Word or another AI model. It's the direction of the platform itself. Microsoft Copilot is steadily evolving from something employees ask questions of into something they work alongside across Microsoft 365. That means successful adoption increasingly needs to be considered at four levels: Individual Productivity How does Copilot help one person work faster and make better decisions? Collaborative Productivity How does it improve meetings, shared documents, knowledge and teamwork? Workflow Productivity Which repeatable business processes could Copilot and agents improve? Organisational Adoption Do we have the right licences, skills, governance, data and measurement in place? What Should Organisations Do Now? My advice is not to rush out and enable every new Copilot feature simply because Microsoft releases it. Start with the business problem, not the feature. Leadership teams should be asking: Are employees genuinely using the Copilot licences we already have? Do people know when to use Copilot Chat versus in-app Copilot? Which roles and teams have the strongest business use cases? Where could Copilot improve an entire workflow rather than a single task? Do employees understand the potential of Copilot Agents? Are our governance, permissions and data foundations ready? Can we measure adoption and business value? The objective shouldn't be to deploy as much AI as possible. It should be to identify the smallest set of capabilities that creates meaningful business value — and build from there. My Advice Three years into the Copilot journey, I think organisations need to change how they think about adoption. Buying licences and teaching people a few prompts isn't enough. The organisations that create the greatest value will be those that identify meaningful use cases, train people around their actual roles and workflows, improve collaboration, experiment carefully with agents and measure what changes. The future of Copilot isn't about running more prompts. It's about redesigning work. Want to Improve Microsoft Copilot Adoption? Photograph: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/Shutterstock AI (artificial intelligence) This article is more than 2 months old Anthropic to disable its most advanced AI models after US order limiting foreign access This article is more than 2 months old Company said US government believes safeguards can be bypassed and product used to identify software vulnerabilities Reuters Sat 13 Jun 2026 08.37 EDT Last modified on Tue 16 Jun 2026 11.40 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Anthropic said it will “abruptly disable” its most advanced AI models for all users after the US government ordered it to suspend access to the models for foreign nationals, citing national security concerns. The company received the export control directive to suspend access to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for all foreign nationals, without being given specific details of the national security concern, Anthropic said in a statement. It is Anthropic’s understanding that the government believes there is a method of bypassing, or “jailbreaking”, a safeguard that would prevent Fable 5 from being used in identifying software vulnerabilities, the company said. Musk’s xAI fired engineer for raising concerns about Grok chatbot, lawsuit claims Read more The order comes just as a previous dispute between Trump administration officials and IPO-bound Anthropic showed signs of easing across parts of the US government. Anthropic’s relationship with the government ruptured this year after it refused to allow the US military to use its AI models for domestic surveillance and fully autonomous weapons systems. The government responded by putting Anthropic on a supply chain blacklist, set to take effect later in the year. The action also marks a major escalation of US efforts to halt foreign adversaries’ AI capabilities. For years, US export controls have focused on the chips and tools that power AI rather than on restricting foreign access to AI itself. Anthropic said the government has given it only “verbal evidence of a potential narrow, non-universal jailbreak”. “We disagree that the finding of a narrow potential jailbreak should be cause for recalling a commercial model deployed to hundreds of millions of people,” the company said. The government directive and Anthropic’s response highlight growing tension between AI developers and regulators over how to assess risks from so-called “jailbreaks”, or methods used to bypass model safeguards. As recently as Wednesday, Anthropic had called for greater US oversight of AI, including the ability to block models with unacceptable risks. It said, however, the government action on Friday did not follow principles of fair and fact-based regulation. The Pentagon’s chief information officer, Kirsten Davies, said in a post on X that the defense department supported prioritizing national security. “Some things are simply more important than revenue cycles, clickbait and pre-IPO valuation. America First. Always,” Davies said. Anthropic confidentially filed for a US IPO last month, edging ahead of rival OpenAI in the race to reach public markets. Earlier this week, Anthropic rolled out an AI model named Claude Fable 5, representing a new tier of capability it calls “Mythos-class”. The model is accompanied by guardrails barring its use in risky areas such as cybersecurity, which some users have complained are “overly broad”, Anthropic said. Experts have said that Mythos models, in the wrong hands, could dramatically accelerate sophisticated cyber-attacks, particularly in sectors such as banking that rely on complex, interconnected and often decades-old technology systems. Anthropic said it had worked with the US government, among others, on safety ahead of the Fable launch and that models from rival AI providers showed a similar ability to unearth minor bugs in code. “The net effect of this order is that we must abruptly disable Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for all our customers to ensure compliance. Access to all other Anthropic models will not be affected,” Anthropic said. Anthropic said that it believed there was a “misunderstanding” and that it is working to restore access to the models as soon as possible. A US official confirmed that the commerce department had issued an export control directive to suspend all access to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 by foreign nationals. sources.title: Microsoft Ads August Update: PMax Previews, AI Visibility
sources.excerpt: Microsoft brought Ad Preview Hub to Performance Max and added Topic Insights to Clarity. Two answers to one complaint, and both need setup work.
sources.content_text: Services AI Tools Blog About Contact Log in Start engines Home / Blog / Marketing / Microsoft Ads August Update Marketing Playbook 10 min read Published August 14, 2026 PMax previews on 3 surfaces · Topic Insights in free Clarity · staged rollout, not full GA Microsoft Ads August Update: PMax Previews, AI Visibility Two Microsoft Advertising announcements, fifteen days apart, answer the same buyer complaint. On July 28 the Ad Preview Hub reached Performance Max, showing auto-assembled creative before it spends. On August 12, Microsoft Clarity added Topic Insights — AI citations grouped by topic, with grounding queries and Share of Authority. Here’s what each one does, what’s actually live, and what to change in your workflow. DA Digital Applied Team Senior strategists · Published Aug 14, 2026 Published Aug 14, 2026 Read time 10 min Sources Microsoft Advertising + trade press PMax preview surfaces 3 MSN · Bing Search · Outlook Preview link lifespan 30 d view-only · no account login Clarity Topic Insights Aug 12 AI Visibility announcement Gap between the two 15 days Jul 28 → Aug 12, 2026 Table of contents 00 Key takeaways 01 What happened, and when 02 Topic Insights in Clarity 03 Ad Preview Hub reaches PMax 04 Links, expiry & staged rollout 05 Uplift & upgrade experiments 06 The black box, both ends 07 What to do this week 08 Conclusion 09 FAQ Microsoft Ads shipped two updates in its August 2026 cycle that attack the same problem from opposite ends: Performance Max campaigns you cannot see into. The Ad Preview Hub now renders PMax creative before it spends, and Microsoft Clarity’s new Topic Insights shows which topics AI answers cite your brand for — and which ones they don’t. The complaint both updates answer is familiar to anyone running Performance Max on either Microsoft or Google. PMax assembles creative automatically from a pooled asset library, across formats and placements, and historically the first time you saw the final rendered combination was after the campaign started spending. At the same time, a growing share of discovery now happens inside AI-generated answers, where advertisers have had almost no visibility into whether their brand appears at all. Invisible creative on one side, invisible AI attribution on the other. This post covers what each announcement actually contains, the precise dates (the trade press has been sloppier about this than usual), the rollout caveats Microsoft’s own channels are candid about, and a practical playbook for what to change in your Microsoft Ads workflow this week. Key takeaways 01 Two announcements, fifteen days apart — not one event. The Ad Preview Hub expansion to Performance Max was announced July 27–28, 2026. The Clarity AI Visibility update with Topic Insights landed August 12, 2026 on Microsoft’s own blog. August round-ups that merge them into one drop are misdating the first. 02 PMax previews now cover three publisher surfaces. MSN, Bing Search, and Outlook — Bing Search is the new addition. Previews are accessed from the asset group editor via a Preview ads button, with device, publisher, asset-type, and extension filters plus a Full view publisher mock-up. 03 Topic Insights groups AI citations by subject. Inside free Microsoft Clarity, the expanded AI Visibility reporting adds grounding queries (the sub-queries an AI generates from one prompt), citation share, and Share of Authority — how often your domain is cited versus competitors within a topic. 04 Shareable preview links are view-only and die in 30 days. No Microsoft Advertising login is needed to open one, only the link generator and their recipients can access it, and it expires after 30 days — so treat links as a sign-off mechanism, not a permanent audit trail. 05 The PMax preview rollout is staged, not full GA. Trade coverage in early August describes some Performance Max accounts enabled with the remainder pending access. Verify availability in your own account before building it into a client workflow or a pitch. 01 — The Timeline What happened, and when . Precision on dates matters here, because most of the “Microsoft Ads August update” framing circulating in aggregator round-ups is actually two distinct announcements roughly two weeks apart. The Performance Max preview news broke first: Search Engine Land covered it on July 27, 2026 , and Navah Hopkins, Microsoft Advertising’s Ads Liaison, announced it on LinkedIn on July 28. The genuinely-August item is the Clarity AI Visibility post Microsoft published on August 12, 2026 , under Hopkins’ byline, introducing Topic Insights. Search Engine Journal’s synthesis treats the AI Visibility reporting, new Performance Max testing tools, and the creative preview updates as one coordinated Microsoft Advertising update cycle — which is fair as a framing, as long as each piece keeps its own date. Here is the shape of the two threads: Jul 27–28, 2026 Ad Preview Hub → Performance Max MSN · Bing Search · Outlook The preview tool that launched for other campaign types in February 2026 extends to PMax, adding Bing Search results-page previews to the MSN and Outlook coverage it already had. Staged rollout — some accounts enabled, others pending. Announced via LinkedIn + trade press Aug 12, 2026 Clarity AI Visibility · Topic Insights Grounding queries · Citation share · Share of Authority Microsoft Clarity’s AI Visibility reporting expands with Topic Insights — AI citations grouped by subject — pitched explicitly at paid-media teams, not just SEO. Free, live in Clarity, with a walkthrough webinar scheduled for August 27. about.ads.microsoft.com · primary source Fifteen days separate the two announcements, and they came through different channels — a liaison LinkedIn post amplified by trade press for the preview expansion, a first-party Microsoft Advertising blog post for the Clarity update. That difference matters when you are deciding how much weight to put on each detail, which is why the sections below flag what is Microsoft-stated, what is independently confirmed, and what is press-reported only. 02 — The August News Topic Insights: AI citations, grouped by subject . The August 12 post — titled “Understand how humans and AI find and choose your brand with Microsoft Clarity” — introduces an expanded AI Visibility reporting layer inside Clarity, Microsoft’s free behavioral-analytics tool. The centerpiece is Topic Insights : AI citations grouped by subject, so a marketer can see which topics their brand is associated with in AI-generated answers, and — often more useful — which topics it is absent from. Three metrics travel with it. Grounding queries expose the specific sub-queries an AI system generates when it fans out a single user prompt into multiple searches — the closest thing yet to a query report for AI answers. Citation share measures how often your content is cited. And Share of Authority compares how often your domain is cited relative to competitors within a topic — a share-of-voice analogue for the AI answer layer. New metric Share of Authority SoA How often a domain is cited relative to competitors within a topic. A competitor-benchmarked AI-citation metric, shipped inside a free analytics tool. Per topic, vs competitors New report Topic Insights Topics AI citations grouped by subject. Shows the topics AI answers associate with your brand — and the gaps where competitors get cited and you don’t. Inside Microsoft Clarity New signal Grounding queries Fan-out The sub-queries an AI system generates from a single prompt before composing its answer. A window into how AI systems actually retrieve your category. Per-prompt retrieval detail Two practical notes. First, Clarity is free, and the announcement gates none of this behind a paid tier or waitlist — which makes it the lowest-friction AI-visibility baseline available to most teams today. Second, Microsoft has scheduled a webinar for August 27, 2026 to walk through the new reporting, worth a calendar slot if AI visibility is landing on your quarterly agenda. If you already track Clarity’s existing AI-citation tracking , Topic Insights sits directly on top of that baseline — same tool, one layer of aggregation up. And on the Bing side, citation-share reporting in Bing Webmaster Tools complements the new Share of Authority metric with a search-console view of the same phenomenon. The positioning line Microsoft is using for this cycle, attributed to Hopkins in trade coverage of the update, is “building with you, not just for you.” Strip the marketing and there is a real signal underneath: the AI Visibility work is aimed at advertisers’ measurement anxiety, not at another automation surface. That is a notable choice of direction for an ads platform in 2026. 03 — The July Context Ad Preview Hub reaches Performance Max . The Ad Preview Hub itself is not new — it first launched for non-PMax campaign types in February 2026 , previously limited to Audience ads. What changed in late July is the campaign type that matters most: Performance Max, the format where auto-assembled creative made previewing simultaneously most necessary and least available. The expansion also added Bing Search results-page previews to the MSN and Outlook coverage the hub already had, bringing PMax preview coverage to three publisher surfaces. Mechanically, per ppc.land’s product walkthrough , the tool is accessed from the asset group editor via a “Preview ads” button. Dropdown filters cover device (Computer or Smartphone), publisher, asset type, and extensions, and a “Full view” toggle renders the ad inside a mock-up of the actual publisher page rather than as an isolated creative unit. For anyone who has tried to explain to a client why their PMax ad “looks different on MSN,” that last detail is the useful one. Why does a preview button deserve this much attention? Because of what Performance Max is. PMax assembles creative automatically from pooled assets across formats and placements — on Google and Microsoft alike — and advertisers historically could not see the final rendered combination before the campaign started spending. Microsoft’s stated rationale for the feature is exactly this gap: reducing reliance on manual screenshots or third-party creative-approval tools for stakeholder, legal, and brand sign-off. “PMax needs flexibility to adapt to AI surfaces.” — Navah Hopkins, Ads Liaison, Microsoft Advertising, LinkedIn (July 28, 2026) Hopkins’ framing places the preview expansion inside the same story as the Clarity work: as ad serving spreads across AI-shaped surfaces, the assembly logic gets more dynamic, and the case for letting advertisers inspect output before spend gets stronger, not weaker. Read together, the two July–August threads are less “two features” than one editorial position about what automation owes its buyers. 04 — Fine Print Shareable links, 30-day expiry, and a staged rollout. The sharing model is the most agency-relevant part of the preview release. Preview links are view-only , require no Microsoft Advertising account access to open, and expire after 30 days . On access control, Hopkins was specific: “Ad Preview Hub allows you to see previews of all asset types on eligible surfaces and devices. This view makes it easier to get sign off on creative with stakeholders and clients through a sharable link. No one except the link generator and those who get sent the link can access the link.” The 30-day expiry deserves more attention than the coverage gave it. If your client-approval workflow treats the preview link as the record of what was approved, that record self-destructs in a month. The practical pattern: use the link for the sign-off moment, then capture screenshots (or export the approval into whatever system holds your paper trail) for anything you might need to reference in a quarter-end dispute. Microsoft also maintains a help-center walkthrough of the hub, linked from Hopkins’ announcement, for the full click-path. Rollout caveat Ad Preview Hub for Performance Max is a staged rollout , not a simultaneous global GA. As of early-August trade coverage, the feature was live for Audience campaigns with some Performance Max accounts enabled and the remainder pending access. Before you tell a client “we can preview this now,” open the asset group editor in their account and confirm the Preview ads button is actually there. 05 — Press-Reported PMax uplift and upgrade experiments. The third thread in the August cycle, reported by Search Engine Journal and other outlets, is an expansion of Performance Max experimentation: “uplift” experiments that measure the impact of adding PMax alongside existing campaigns, and “upgrade” experiments that compare existing Search or Shopping campaigns against a PMax migration. A caveat worth stating plainly: this experiments news traces to press coverage rather than a first-party Microsoft URL, so treat the details as press-reported until the help docs catch up. The same coverage reports recommended prerequisites of roughly 30 conversions in the prior 30 days and a test window of 4 to 12 weeks — again per the press writeups, not a Microsoft page we could verify. Directionally both figures are consistent with how conversion-based experimentation works everywhere: below a minimum conversion volume, an uplift test cannot separate signal from noise inside a practical timeframe. If you want the structured version of that discipline, our PMax asset-testing playbook covers hypothesis design, holdout structure, and when to call a test — all of it transferable to Microsoft’s uplift and upgrade formats as they arrive. The experiments thread matters strategically because it addresses the third classic PMax complaint after invisible creative and invisible attribution: unprovable incrementality. An advertiser who can preview the creative, see the AI-citation footprint, and run a controlled uplift test against their existing campaign structure is dealing with a materially less opaque product than the PMax of 2024–2025. 06 — Original Analysis The PMax black box, addressed from both ends . The trade coverage groups the two as one update cycle without connecting the mechanics, so here is the synthesis: the Ad Preview Hub expansion and Topic Insights are the same product decision expressed twice. PMax’s core buyer objection has always been opacity — you cannot see what it will show, and you cannot see where its results come from. July’s announcement opens the creative black box; August’s opens the attribution one. The table below maps the shift as a working capability audit for PMax buyers. The three Performance Max visibility blind spots on Microsoft Advertising, what each looked like before the July–August 2026 update cycle, the new capability that addresses it, and the workflow change advertisers should make. Synthesis by Digital Applied from Microsoft Advertising announcements and trade coverage, August 2026. Blind spot Before this cycle After this cycle What to change Creative rendering PMax assembled headlines, images, and descriptions from a pooled asset library across formats and placements. The first time most advertisers saw the final rendered combination was after the campaign had started spending. Ad Preview Hub renders asset-group combinations across MSN, Bing Search, and Outlook, filtered by device, publisher, asset type, and extensions, with a Full view mock-up of the actual publisher page. Add a per-asset-group preview pass to the launch checklist. Catch broken crops and off-brand pairings before budget flows, not after. AI-citation attribution Clarity’s earlier AI-visibility layer surfaced citations, but without topic grouping teams could not see which subjects their brand was winning or losing inside AI-generated answers. Topic Insights groups AI citations by subject, alongside grounding queries, citation share, and a Share of Authority metric that compares your domain’s citation frequency against competitors within a topic. Baseline Share of Authority on your revenue topics now, then brief content and paid media around the topics where the brand is absent. Stakeholder sign-off Creative approval for PMax meant manual screenshots or third-party approval tools, because there was no reliable way to show a client or legal team what the campaign would actually serve. View-only shareable preview links that require no Microsoft Advertising login, restricted to the link generator and their recipients, expiring after 30 days. Fold preview links into the client-approval workflow, but archive screenshots for the audit trail — the link itself is gone in 30 days. Projecting forward, the interesting question is whether this becomes the competitive axis between Microsoft and Google on automated campaign types. Google’s PMax has moved in the same direction — more reporting, more controls — but Microsoft pairing creative preview with a free, competitor-benchmarked AI-citation report is a distinct posture: transparency as the differentiator for the second-place ads platform. If Share of Authority data starts showing up in quarterly business reviews the way share-of-voice data does today, this August cycle will look like the starting point. 07 — Playbook What to do this week . Four moves, in priority order — all doable with existing budgets and the tools as they stand today: Everyone Baseline Topic Insights in Clarity Clarity is free and the AI Visibility reporting is live now. Record Share of Authority on your revenue topics before you change anything, so every later content or paid-media move has a before number. Do first — 30 minutes PMax advertisers Check for the Preview ads button Open the asset group editor in each Microsoft Ads account you run. Staged rollout means some accounts have it and some don’t — know which of yours do before you build it into a client workflow. Do this week Agencies Rebuild the sign-off workflow Replace screenshot decks with view-only preview links for client and legal approval — and add a screenshot-archive step, because links expire after 30 days and your audit trail shouldn’t. Process change Growth teams Queue an uplift experiment When the press-reported uplift/upgrade experiments reach your account, test PMax incrementality against your existing Search and Shopping structure instead of trusting blended numbers. Watch + prepare Two adjacent hygiene checks make all of this land better. If your PMax campaigns run on Shopping feeds, diagnosing PMax feed issues in Product Explorer before you start previewing creative saves you from approving ads whose underlying products are disapproved. And if the platform work is stacking up faster than your team can absorb it, our paid media services cover exactly this kind of platform-update triage — deciding which of a month’s announcements deserve workflow changes and which are noise. 08 — Conclusion Transparency as the product strategy . The shape of the update Microsoft is answering PMax’s trust problem from both ends — creative and attribution. The August 2026 Microsoft Ads cycle is best understood as one argument in two parts. The July 27–28 Ad Preview Hub expansion lets Performance Max advertisers see auto-assembled creative on MSN, Bing Search, and Outlook before it spends. The August 12 Clarity update gives the same advertisers Topic Insights — AI citations grouped by subject, with grounding queries and Share of Authority — for free. Both address the same buyer complaint: automation you cannot inspect . The caveats are real and worth respecting. The PMax preview rollout is staged, so availability varies by account. Preview links expire after 30 days, so they are a sign-off mechanism, not an archive. And the uplift/upgrade experiment details — including the reported conversion thresholds — remain press-sourced until Microsoft’s own documentation catches up. None of that diminishes the direction; it just tells you where to double-check before promising capabilities to stakeholders. The practical move is unglamorous: baseline your Share of Authority now, confirm preview access in each account you run, and rebuild the creative sign-off workflow around links-plus-archives. Teams that do those three things this month will spend the rest of the quarter making decisions with data their competitors are still waiting for. sources.title: Major layoffs of 2026: Amazon, Meta, Oracle, Microsoft and more
sources.excerpt: From Amazon and Oracle to Meta, Microsoft and Etsy, here are 20 major layoffs announced or carried out in 2026 through August.
sources.content_text: Close Menu Facebook X (Twitter) Instagram Facebook X (Twitter) YouTube Subscribe Sunday, August 16 HOME BUSINESS STARTUPS TECHNOLOGY INTERVIEWS OPINION IMMIGRATION AB PODCASTS AB EVENTS --> Home » Major layoffs of 2026: Amazon, Meta, Oracle, Microsoft and more --> Major layoffs of 2026: Amazon, Meta, Oracle, Microsoft and more By Jayujyoti Mullick August 9, 2026 Updated: August 9, 2026 9 Mins Read Share Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Email The U.S. labor market has continued to see significant workforce reductions in 2026, particularly in technology. While artificial intelligence has become an important part of the restructuring narrative, companies have also cited cost controls, organizational changes, changing business priorities and the need to operate with smaller teams. The American Bazaar’s coverage has tracked several of these layoffs, particularly where they affect technology workers and Indian professionals in the United States. Here are some of the most significant layoffs announced or carried out between January and August 2026. 1. Amazon: 16,000 jobs, January Amazon announced about 16,000 corporate layoffs in January, bringing the company’s total corporate job cuts since October 2025 to approximately 30,000. The company described the restructuring as an effort to reduce organizational layers, increase ownership and eliminate bureaucracy. The cuts affected multiple divisions, including AWS, Alexa, Prime Video, devices, advertising and other corporate functions. The reduction represented roughly 10% of Amazon’s corporate workforce and became one of the largest corporate workforce reductions in the company’s history. 2. Amazon: another 2,200 jobs, February Amazon’s restructuring continued into February. A Washington state WARN filing showed that Amazon planned to eliminate 2,200 positions in Washington, with the job separations scheduled to begin in April. The cuts included 401 positions associated with facility closures. Amazon’s January and February reductions highlighted how the company’s workforce restructuring extended beyond a single round of corporate layoffs. 3. Block: 4,000 jobs, February Jack Dorsey’s payments company Block announced plans to eliminate about 4,000 jobs, nearly half of its workforce. Dorsey explicitly linked the restructuring to advances in AI and productivity tools, arguing that smaller teams using AI could accomplish more work. The announcement came shortly after Block reported quarterly revenue above Wall Street expectations, making the scale of the workforce reduction particularly notable. 4. Salesforce: fewer than 1,000 jobs, February Salesforce eliminated fewer than 1,000 positions in February across areas including marketing, product management, data analytics and its Agentforce AI unit. The company said AI-driven efficiencies had reduced the number of support cases and meant that some support engineering positions no longer needed to be backfilled. Salesforce’s cuts were part of a broader restructuring around AI and automation. 5. Amazon Robotics: at least 100 jobs, March Amazon’s restructuring reached its robotics organization in March, with at least 100 white-collar positions eliminated. The affected unit works on autonomous systems and fulfillment-center technology. Amazon described robotics as a strategic priority even as it reduced staffing within the division. The cuts illustrated one of the defining contradictions of 2026: companies are investing heavily in automation while also reducing the number of people working on related operations. 6. Oracle: tens of thousands of jobs, March-April Oracle became one of the year’s most significant layoff stories. Reports in March said Oracle was preparing to eliminate thousands of jobs as it dealt with the enormous cost of expanding its AI infrastructure. By April, estimates put the global cuts at up to 30,000 positions, including roughly 12,000 in India, although the exact number was initially based on estimates rather than a single companywide announcement. Oracle subsequently disclosed in its annual report that its workforce had fallen from approximately 162,000 to 141,000, a decline of about 21,000 employees over the fiscal year. Because the figures were reported at different stages, the 21,000 figure is the more firmly documented companywide number. 7. Meta: about 8,000 jobs, announced April, implemented May Meta announced plans to cut approximately 8,000 jobs, or about 10% of its workforce. The company said the layoffs were part of a restructuring designed to make the organization more efficient while redirecting resources toward artificial intelligence. The layoffs began on May 20, with notifications sent to employees in multiple waves. Meta also planned to move thousands of employees into AI-related initiatives and reduce management layers. 8. Snap: about 1,000 jobs, April Snap announced approximately 1,000 layoffs, equivalent to about 16% of its full-time workforce. The Snapchat parent also closed more than 300 open positions as part of a restructuring focused on improving efficiency and reducing costs. Snap said AI was allowing the company to operate with smaller teams, with more than 65% of new code being generated using AI tools. 9. Walmart: 1,000 corporate jobs, May Walmart eliminated about 1,000 corporate positions in May as it simplified its organizational structure. The retail giant’s restructuring was notable because Walmart did not identify AI as the primary reason for the cuts. Instead, the company pointed to organizational changes and efforts to simplify its operations. 10. LinkedIn: workforce reductions, May LinkedIn, owned by Microsoft, also reduced its workforce in May as Microsoft intensified its focus on cost controls and AI-related investments. The American Bazaar reported the cuts as part of a broader restructuring across Microsoft’s operations. LinkedIn’s reductions illustrate that the AI-driven restructuring trend has extended beyond Microsoft’s core software and cloud businesses. 11. Cisco: fewer than 4,000 jobs, May Cisco announced that it would reduce its workforce by fewer than 4,000 employees, representing less than 5% of its workforce. The networking company said the changes were designed to align its workforce and cost structure with strategic growth opportunities, including AI, silicon, optics and security.The company announced while reporting strong quarterly financial results, underscoring how layoffs in 2026 have not necessarily been limited to companies facing financial distress. 12. Groupon: up to 400 jobs, May Groupon announced plans to eliminate up to 400 positions, nearly a quarter of its workforce. The company described the restructuring as part of its effort to become more AI-focused, with automation expected to take on functions including lead generation, customer support and internal operations. 13. ClickUp: 22% of workforce, May Productivity software company ClickUp cut about 22% of its workforce in May. The company framed the reduction as a strategic reorganization around AI rather than a conventional cost-cutting exercise. Reports put the affected workforce at roughly 290 employees. The announcement became one of the more prominent examples of a technology company explicitly arguing that AI enables a smaller workforce to produce more output. 14. Acrisure: 2,250 jobs, May onward Insurance technology company Acrisure announced plans to eliminate approximately 2,250 jobs through 2027, or close to 11% of its workforce. The restructuring was linked to increased use of AI and automation across the company. Unlike a single-day mass layoff, Acrisure’s reduction is being implemented over a longer period. 15. Oracle: 21,000 jobs confirmed, June Oracle’s June disclosure provided a clearer picture of the scale of its restructuring. The company reported that its workforce had fallen by approximately 21,000 employees over the fiscal year, or about 13%. Oracle attributed the restructuring to several factors, including management and product changes, strategic shifts, acquisitions, employee performance issues and, in part, AI adoption. The cuts came as Oracle was simultaneously committing tens of billions of dollars to expanding AI-focused cloud infrastructure. 16. Microsoft: about 4,800 jobs, July Microsoft eliminated roughly 4,800 positions, or about 2.1% of its global workforce, in July. The cuts affected several areas, with Xbox particularly affected. Microsoft eliminated about 1,600 Xbox positions in the round. The layoffs followed earlier reductions and came as Microsoft continued to commit substantial resources to AI infrastructure and services. The American Bazaar reported the July cuts as affecting approximately 4,000 employees, while later reporting put the figure closer to 4,800. 17. Xbox: 3,200 additional jobs planned, July Microsoft’s gaming division faced another major restructuring in July. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma told employees that approximately 3,200 positions could be eliminated during fiscal 2027, including about 1,600 immediate cuts. The announcement followed Microsoft’s broader workforce reductions and restructuring of several Xbox studios. 18. Sprout Social: 260 jobs, July Sprout Social announced plans to eliminate approximately 260 positions as it restructured around changes in the software industry and expanded its AI capabilities. The company expected the restructuring to generate between $18 million and $20 million in pretax charges, largely related to severance and employee benefits. 19. Intel: additional cuts, July Intel announced another restructuring affecting its Data Center Group in July. The chipmaker did not disclose a specific number of jobs affected by the latest round, but the company said it was seeking a more focused and efficient organization. Intel’s latest cuts came after the company had already reduced its global workforce by roughly 40,000 employees over the previous two years, making the latest restructuring part of a much larger turnaround effort. 20. Etsy: 220 jobs, August Etsy became one of the latest major companies to announce layoffs in 2026. The online marketplace said on Aug. 5 that it would eliminate approximately 220 positions, representing about 12% of its workforce. Most of the affected positions are in product and engineering. CEO Kruti Patel Goyal said the restructuring was not driven by AI or cost-cutting, but by an effort to simplify the organization, improve coordination and accelerate decision-making. The announcement came even as Etsy reported stronger-than-expected second-quarter results, making it another example of layoffs being used as part of organizational restructuring rather than solely as a response to weak financial performance. What the 2026 layoffs show The 2026 layoff cycle has a more complicated story than simply “AI is taking jobs.” Artificial intelligence has been explicitly cited in several major workforce reductions. Block, Snap, Groupon and ClickUp are among the clearest examples. Amazon, Meta, Oracle and Microsoft have also been restructuring while simultaneously increasing their AI investments. But companies have also stressed other reasons. Etsy, for example, explicitly said its August layoffs were not driven by AI or cost-cutting. Oracle cited a combination of organizational, product, strategic and acquisition-related changes, alongside AI adoption. The broader trend also extends well beyond Silicon Valley. Retail, finance, insurance and other industries have announced significant workforce reductions during the year. Current tracking data from TrueUp lists 520 technology layoff events affecting about 174,721 workers in 2026 as of the latest update. At the same time, Challenger, Gray & Christmas data cited by The Wall Street Journal showed that U.S. employers had announced about 33,500 job cuts in July, while total 2026 layoffs through that point were lower than during the same period in 2025. The technology sector nevertheless accounted for more than 30% of announced cuts. For Indian American and other immigrant technology workers, the consequences can extend beyond unemployment. The American Bazaar has reported cases in which layoffs at companies such as Meta have put H-1B worker s at risk of losing their status if they cannot find another sponsoring employer within the applicable grace period. The pattern suggests that the 2026 workforce story is not simply about companies becoming unprofitable. Increasingly, employers are redesigning organizations around smaller teams, automation, AI tools and different capital priorities. For workers, however, the distinction between an AI-driven restructuring and a conventional layoff may matter less when the result is the same: a job disappears. As of this page's 14 August 2026 evidence cutoff, Sam Altman is the co-founder and chief executive officer of OpenAI. OpenAI names him as co-founder and CEO in its 27 February 2026 company publication, which is the primary record used here. The answer is dated deliberately: executive roles can change, and a current-role page should show readers exactly when and where the fact was verified. The concentration has a cost that is easy to miss while it is working. Demand attached to a person does not transfer when the person does, it carries whatever reputation the person carries that week, and it competes with the company's own pages in results the company would otherwise own. This piece traces how the concentration forms, what it does to discovery, and what a brand can do about it before the question becomes urgent. What the latest official record does and does not establish The cited OpenAI publication establishes the role because the company names Altman directly as co-founder and CEO in a dated corporate announcement. It does not make every surrounding claim about OpenAI, the AI market, or a future release automatically true. Role verification and claim verification are separate jobs: the first can be resolved from the maintained company record, while the second requires the original product note, agreement, evaluation, policy text, or partner statement connected to the specific claim. That distinction also keeps the page useful when a search spike has no single confirmed trigger. VJOURNAL can update the evidence cutoff and link a material new record without rewriting the profile as though attention itself were an event. If the role changes, the direct answer changes. If a model, partnership, or policy changes, that development belongs in dated context with its own evidence. The profile remains the stable route between the executive query and those narrower records. Why Sam Altman keeps trending in 2026 Why Sam Altman keeps trending in 2026 is best understood as a category question rather than a celebrity question. OpenAI identifies Altman as its co-founder and chief executive in current company material. The role connects one person to decisions about models, products, infrastructure partnerships, safety commitments, enterprise adoption, and the public explanation of where advanced AI may go next. Users searching his name are often trying to reduce uncertainty about OpenAI itself. They may want to know who leads the company, what a new statement means, how a partnership changes capacity, or whether a product direction signals a wider change in the AI market. The executive name becomes a compact route into a technical and institutional story that would otherwise require several separate searches. OpenAI leadership now spans several audiences An AI company speaks to more audiences at once than a typical software vendor. Developers want capability and reliability. Companies want cost, security, governance, and continuity. Policymakers want accountability. Researchers look for evidence about progress and limitations. Individual users want tools that are understandable and useful. A leadership statement can therefore trigger different interpretations across every one of these groups. This is why a page about Altman should not collapse all interest into personal biography. The search intent is usually tied to a decision: whether to adopt a product, trust a direction, understand a policy position, or anticipate a change in the competitive landscape. Strong coverage names the audience and decision under discussion instead of presenting general fame as though it were the explanation. Product releases turn executives into distribution nodes In platform markets, leadership communication is part of distribution. A model or product announcement reaches developers, enterprise buyers, creators, educators, and regulators through different channels, yet many of those groups return to the same executive interview or company statement for context. The leader becomes a reference point through which technical change is translated into a story about timing, access, risk, and expected use. When reading any executive position, the practical test is whether responsibility, evaluation, escalation, and monitoring are visible at the workflow level. Extract the concrete commitments and separate them from forecasts. If another organization is named, check its own announcement because scope, timing, and responsibilities may be described differently. For technical claims, look for documentation, evaluations, system cards, or reproducible examples. For governance claims, look for named processes and accountable owners. For infrastructure claims, distinguish announced investment from deployed capacity. This method is slower than repeating an executive quote and faster than correcting a page built on an inference the source never actually made. What teams should monitor instead of personality A company deciding whether to build on an AI platform needs a compact monitoring list: model availability, pricing, latency, evaluation results on its own tasks, data-handling terms, regional access, rate limits, incident communication, and migration options. Leadership matters because it shapes priorities, but operational dependence should be managed through documented product behavior and contracts rather than confidence in one public figure. The same principle applies to media analysis. Attention can reveal which issues audiences find uncertain, but it cannot substitute for evidence about adoption or performance. The article should identify the trigger and then move quickly to the documents that help a reader make a decision. Product capability, business structure, infrastructure, governance, copyright, labor impact, and national policy continue to change together. As long as OpenAI remains influential across those surfaces, statements by its chief executive will be interpreted as signals about more than one company. Durability does not mean every headline has equal value. The highest-value pages will be those that keep a stable question, update the evidence, and resist converting every new appearance into a separate thin article. Amazon Raises 2026 AI Spending to $220B: Smart Bet or Riskier Trap? 3 min read AMZN Amazon AMZN has pushed its 2026 capital expenditure forecast to roughly $220 billion, up from the $200 billion guided earlier in the year, with the increase tied primarily to higher memory and component costs and continued build-out of AI and cloud infrastructure. The revised outlook, disclosed alongside second-quarter 2026 results, underscores how central artificial intelligence has become to Amazon's growth story, even as the bill for that ambition keeps climbing. The spending case is being backed by numbers that are hard to dismiss. AWS revenues rose 36.7% year over year in the second quarter to $42.2 billion, its fastest pace in 18 quarters and the fifth straight quarter of acceleration, pushing the segment to a $169 billion annualized run rate. AWS operating margin expanded to 39%, up roughly 650 basis points from a year earlier, suggesting that scale and efficiency gains are outpacing the cost of new capacity. The unit's backlog — customer commitments for future work — swelled to $496 billion, more than doubling over the past year and giving management visibility into demand well beyond this year's spending cycle. Company leadership has said capacity for 2027 is largely already spoken for, with some 2028 demand already committed, a sign that the infrastructure being funded now is not speculative. Company-wide, the quarter reinforced the momentum: net sales climbed 20% to $200.6 billion, and operating income jumped 43% to $27.5 billion. Guidance for the third quarter calls for net sales of $197 billion to $202 billion and operating income of $22.5 billion to $26.5 billion, with management attributing the sequential slowdown mainly to Prime Day timing shifts and currency effects rather than any softening in underlying demand. Custom silicon adds another dimension to the wager. Amazon's in-house Trainium and Graviton chips have already crossed a $20 billion-plus annual run rate, and the newly ramped Trainium3 platform is central to expanding compute for AWS' largest AI customers. With demand still outstripping available capacity by the company's own account, the elevated spending looks less like a leap of faith and more like a calculated response to orders already on the books. Rival Cloud Spending: Microsoft and Alphabet Keep Pace Amazon's $220 billion capex plan puts it ahead of rivals Microsoft MSFT and Alphabet GOOGL, though both are scaling aggressively too. Microsoft has guided calendar-year 2026 capital expenditure to roughly $190 billion, with Azure revenue growth around 40% and an approximate $80 billion backlog constrained more by power availability than demand. Alphabet has raised its 2026 capex guidance to $195-$205 billion, as Google Cloud revenues surged 82% year over year, its fastest growth among the three. While Amazon leads in absolute spending, Microsoft and Alphabet's combined outlays underscore that hyperscaler capital intensity is now an industry-wide, not company-specific, phenomenon. OpenAI co-founder John Schulman has announced his departure from the AI start-up to join rival Anthropic. In a note to colleagues shared on X today (6 August), Schulman said his choice to leave OpenAI stems from his “desire to deepen my focus on AI alignment, and to start a new chapter of my career where I can return to hands-on technical work”. “I’ve decided to pursue this goal at Anthropic, where I believe I can gain new perspectives and do research alongside people deeply engaged with the topics I’m most interested in,” Schulman said. “To be clear, I’m not leaving due to lack of support for alignment research at OpenAI. On the contrary, company leaders have been very committed to investing in this area. My decision is a personal one, based on how I want to focus my efforts in the next phase of my career.” Fellow co-founder Greg Brockman, who is also the president of OpenAI, announced around the same time that he is taking a sabbatical through the end of the year. “First time to relax since co-founding OpenAI nine years ago,” Brockman wrote on X. “The mission is far from complete; we still have a safe AGI [artificial general intelligence] to build.” This is not the first time core members of OpenAI have jumped ship to join rival Anthropic. In May, former OpenAI executive Jan Leike left the company to join Anthropic in a similar role. Leike was one of the leaders of OpenAI’s superalignment team, which was focused on the safety of future AI systems. But this team was dissolved after Leike and former OpenAI chief scientist Ilya Sutskever  resigned from the company earlier that month. Leike  spoke out against the company  shortly after resigning, claiming he disagreed with OpenAI’s leadership about the company’s core priorities “for some time” and that these issues had reached a “breaking point”. “I believe much more of our bandwidth should be spent getting ready for the next generations of models, on security, monitoring, preparedness, safety, adversarial robustness, (super)alignment, confidentiality, societal impact and related topics,” he said at the time. Just last month, OpenAI co-founder Andrej Karpathy, who  left the company in February  to work on personal projects, announced a new company called Eureka Labs that will enable students to study a wide variety of subjects through its AI platform. “Thank you for everything you’ve done for OpenAI!” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wrote of Schulman’s departure. “You are a brilliant researcher, a deep thinker about product and society, and mostly, you are a great friend to all of us. We will miss you tremendously and make you proud of this place.” Meanwhile, Elon Musk has revived his lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging that Altman and Brockman have breached the company’s founding contract by placing profits and commercial interests above public good. Musk decided to  sue OpenAI and its CEO Sam Altman  earlier this year for seeking to profit from its AI creations – only to drop it quietly in June. In a lawsuit filed in California yesterday, Musk claims that the two “assiduously manipulated Musk into co-founding their spurious non-profit venture” by promising that OpenAI would be safer and more transparent than profit-driven alternatives. sources.content_text: Advertisement Artificial intelligence Tech Big Tech OpenAI co-founders step back as Schulman leaves for rival Anthropic OpenAI president Greg Brockman is on leave through the end of the year marking a shift for the company with only two members of its founding team left 2 -MIN READ 2 -MIN Bloomberg Published: 1:44pm, 6 Aug 2024 Greg Brockman, the president of OpenAI and a central figure at the company, said he is is going on leave until the end of the year. At the same time, researcher John Schulman is leaving for rival artificial intelligence start-up Anthropic. Both men are OpenAI co-founders, and their moves mark a shift at the company following already significant management churn this year. Peter Deng, a vice-president of product, also left in recent months, a spokesperson said. And earlier this year, several members of the company’s safety teams exited. OpenAI has made key hires, too, recently adding a new chief financial officer and chief product officer. The result is a start-up that looks significantly different than it did a year ago, and from when it launched in 2015. With the absence of Brockman and Schulman, only two members of OpenAI’s original founding team remain: Wojciech Zaremba and chief executive officer Sam Altman. Brockman, who goes by “GDB” to many at the company, was a key ally of Altman when the CEO was briefly ousted last year. Brockman quit in protest after Altman was fired. In a post on X on Monday night, Brockman wrote that the leave would be his first chance to relax since the company’s founding. Schulman, who was a research scientist at the company focused on training its AI models, said in a post on X on Monday that he would focus on safety at Anthropic, but that concerns around that issue didn’t drive his decision to quit. Photograph: Nic Coury/AP Mark Zuckerberg Zuckerberg pushes ‘superintelligent’ AI for all as Meta releases open-weight model Meta CEO presents utopian vision of AI in 6,000-word essay amid Silicon Valley debate over government regulation Nick Robins-Early Mon 10 Aug 2026 18.57 EDT Last modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 12.38 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Mark Zuckerberg published a lengthy essay on Monday detailing his views on artificial intelligence and announced several plans for how Meta would develop the technology in the future. The CEO’s essay went online the same day as Meta released a new, open-weight AI model that seeks to rival Anthropic and OpenAI’s products called Muse Glimmer. Over the course of more than 6,000 words in a post titled The Future is for Everyone, Zuckerberg addressed a range of topics related to AI that included datacenters, government regulation, cybersecurity, the creation of bioweapons, labor market disruption, surveillance powers and more. The essay presented a utopian vision of AI as a personalized “superintelligence” – using the word 60 times. “Some argue that superintelligence itself or a small set of experts who control it should decide what is best for humanity. We disagree,” Zuckerberg wrote. Central to Zuckerberg’s post was an argument for free-to-download, open-weight AI models – like the kind Meta develops – and a lack of government regulation of artificial intelligence. Zuckerberg’s stance sets him and Meta apart from industry leaders OpenAI and Anthropic, which have argued that open-source AI is dangerous. The two frontier labs have released proprietary AI products and argued that cutting-edge models should remain tightly controlled by the companies that build them. Crew of Zuckerberg yacht did not hear radio call to assist boat, Meta says Read more Zuckerberg’s post comes as Silicon Valley is engaged in a heated debate over how to regulate AI development, which has involved the creation of a secret White House framework for testing new models and an ongoing debate over whether to restrict the use of Chinese-made open-source AI. As Anthropic and OpenAI have surged ahead in the AI industry, competitors such as Meta have also grown wary of their dominance and sought to position their open models as alternatives. Zuckerberg framed Meta’s pursuit of open-weight AI as a more democratic version of the technology and one that will create a “balance of power” between users, whether that involves states, companies or individuals. His plans also called for letting users decide what “values” an AI model should have, as opposed to a company encoding it with rigid guardrails and beliefs. An AI agent for all? Try using your brain, Mark Zuckerberg Read more “If the power of superintelligence is held by a small number of individuals, businesses, governments, or AI itself, then that will naturally lead to outcomes that are less favorable for everyone else,” Zuckerberg wrote. Tech leaders have made a cottage industry out of releasing broad, vaguely philosophical treatises on artificial intelligence, which tend to double as marketing materials for their own companies and products. Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Palantir’s Alex Karp and the venture capitalist Marc Andreessen have all written long manifestos on the virtues and dangers of the technology. In addition to weighing in on open-source models, Zuckerberg also called for accelerating the buildout of AI infrastructure such as datacenters . The massive development of resource-hungry datacenters has become a divisive issue in the US, with rapidly growing public opposition and calls from politicians to issue moratoriums on their construction. Zuckerberg wrote in the essay that Meta would create a fund to invest more in local communities near datacenters, ands cited an example from Louisiana where some teachers received a $50,000 bonus check as a result of increased sales tax revenue from the company’s infrastructure investment. On government testing of AI models for cybersecurity risks, a tangible concern after rogue models have hacked outside organizations in recent months, Zuckerberg agreed that companies should share “intermediate training checkpoints and technical staff” but provided few details. He broadly warned that regulation would cause China to overtake the US in the AI race, where he claimed it already has an advantage in terms of building infrastructure. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to TechScape A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion Bernie Sanders calls on Silicon Valley to ‘pause AI development’ in interest of humanity Read more “Any policy that slows American model releases – even by a month – could add significant risk to American leadership while letting foreign models race ahead,” Zuckerberg. Many of Zuckerberg’s policy plans in his essay lacked detail or reiterated previous claims about the abundant wealth and prosperity that AI would create, such as touting that everyone would have “invention superpowers” to create new businesses. His version of the future also is inherently tied to Meta products, such as the company’s AI-enabled smart glasses. “Everyone will have an exceptionally capable personal agent that understands you, your goals, and everything you care about,” Zuckerberg said. “You’ll be able to interact with your agent through any device, including your glasses to keep you present in the moment with the people you care about.” On thornier issues such as loss of jobs from AI, autonomous weapons and government surveillance, Zuckerberg mostly brushed them aside. Law enforcement and the military already possess greater intelligence-gathering powers than the average person, Zuckerberg argued, and this would continue with access to AI. Companies may shrink in size due to AI, he conceded, but the technology would create new economic opportunities. “People will have to adapt, and this will be challenging,” Zuckerberg said about labor disruption from new technology. “But the more that everyone has a personal agent that is superintelligent at teaching us new skills and helping us adapt to change, the smoother this will be.” This article was amended on 12 August 2026. An earlier version of the headline and text said that Meta was releasing an open-source AI model; the company released an open-weight model. novel_idea.topic_thesis: Open weights democratize agency, not control; unless regulatory capacity spreads with capability, a “balance of power” release can widen the gap between who can act and who can correct the consequences.
novel_idea.angle: Decode Meta’s “superintelligence for all” argument as a category error: distributing model access is not the same as distributing the doctrine, evaluations, permissions, feedback paths, and accountability required to govern its use.
novel_idea.hook: Meta says open weights create a balance of power. But downloading the power to act is not the same as downloading the ability to govern what happens next.
novel_idea.argument_summary: Meta links open-weight models to democratization, user-chosen values, and a balance of power among individuals, companies, and states. The Dionysus Program distinguishes agency—the capacity to act—from coherence and regulatory variety—the capacity to keep action bounded, observable, correctable, and accountable. Open weights can spread agency across an ecosystem immediately, but the release itself does not establish doctrine, evaluations, stop conditions, feedback paths, or accountable owners for downstream deployments. Capability can therefore decentralize faster than correction. The operator decision is to evaluate an open-weight release not only by who can access it, but by whether affected actors can bound, audit, stop, and learn from its actions. This differs from prior arguments about agent sprawl inside one organization by moving the mechanism across the organizational boundary and directly challenging the claim that access alone produces a balance of power.
novel_idea.novelty_rationale: The closest post argues that internal agent deployment can outrun an organization’s integration and governance capacity, producing nonlinear overflow. The new argument changes the boundary and consequence: it examines an open-weight model distributed beyond the producer’s organizational perimeter and argues that capability distribution can be mistaken for political or institutional control. Its central test is ecosystem-level distribution of correction capacity, not internal visibility into agent interactions. No prior post challenges democratization claims by separating distributed agency from distributed regulatory variety.
novel_idea.source_grounding: The Guardian reports that Meta paired its open-weight Muse Glimmer release with Zuckerberg’s claim that open models would create a more democratic “balance of power,” allow users to choose model values, and support lighter regulation. The Dionysus Program states that useful autonomous agency requires current doctrine, permissions, evaluations, stop conditions, feedback paths, blast-radius limits, and accountability. Its Ashby-compatible rule holds that regulatory variety must match agency variety; otherwise additional agency produces control loss and incoherence.
